chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1. Note: Concerning one who sells or gives as a gift 'tzon' and owns both sheep and goats, is only the sheep included or also the goats? If the parties speak in the vernacular and write in the vernacular, or conversely speak in Hebrew and write in Hebrew, we follow ordinary human usage, as in the laws of vows, and the same applies to documents. In ordinary usage goats are not included in the term 'tzon,' only sheep. But if they speak in the vernacular and the sale or gift document is written in Hebrew using the word 'tzon,' then goats are included as well. This is learned from the opening Mishnah of the chapter Ma'aser Behemah in Bechorot, where it is explicit that sheep and goats may be tithed together because they are one category of tzon. And none of them contains a quarter kav. It appears that Rama added this limitation because the Mechaber concludes that the purchaser takes those rocky or sunken areas without additional payment, following the Rambam. The Tur cites the Ramah as agreeing, provided no single one contains a quarter kav. If one contains a quarter kav, it is not sold as part of the rest of the beit kor without payment. According to the Rosh and Rashbam, however, who hold that such areas remain the seller's and the purchaser must accept the field with them interspersed within it, even a quarter kav can be present. Proof appears from the Tur's later citation of Ramban, based on the Yerushalmi, that when pits are less than ten handbreadths deep, or rocks less than ten high, they are measured with the field provided no one of them is wider than ten handbreadths or four cubits, according to the respective opinions. He does not place a similar width limitation in the first clause, where they are ten handbreadths deep or high and therefore not measured, yet the purchaser must accept a field interrupted by them. This implies that in the first case even a depression or rock wider than four cubits and even larger than a quarter kav does not void the sale. The Mechaber and Rama omit the Yerushalmi limitation concerning width in the following law, and I do not know why. Perhaps they hold, as Darkei Moshe suggests, that Rashbam disagrees with Ramban. In the Derishah I wrote in the Beit Yosef's name similarly, although in my glosses to Darkei Moshe I questioned where the disagreement lies. Rashbam's statement that a rock ten high is not measured when it is four cubits wide does not necessarily conflict with Ramban's statement that a lower rock is measured up to that width. At first glance Rama may have added the limitation of less than a quarter kav because the Rambam later says that a single rock of a quarter kav has a separate identity and is not sold with the field. Even that is not conclusive, for perhaps there the Rambam means only that it is not counted toward the measured area, while here, where a full beit kor of level ground is separately measured, even a quarter kav obstacle does not void the sale.

chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 24. In the gloss: But if he said, "My property in so-and-so's house," etc. Note: Concerning one who says, "All my property in so-and-so's house," see the Sema and Shach. It appears to me that the law parallels the case of contradictory formulations such as "a kor for thirty, each seah for a sela," where the first and last phrases point in different directions. There is a doubt whether to follow the first expression or the last, and the law therefore follows the party in possession. This resolves the apparent contradictory inferences in the wording of Rabbeinu. If he says only "my property in so-and-so's house," movable property is not included even if the recipient presently possesses it. If he says "all my property" without adding "in so-and-so's house," movable property is included even if the donor remains in possession. But if he says "all my property in so-and-so's house," there is a legal doubt whether the first or last phrase governs, and we follow the possessor. This appears correct.

Within the greater part of the field. The entire field is a beit kor, thirty seah. Its greater portion for this calculation is sixteen seah. The five kav at issue must lie within those sixteen seah. Imagine a long narrow strip extending through the field across sixteen seah, such that if it were cut into small strips and placed side by side in a square it would contain no more than five kav. Four kav of this strip consist of rocks, with one kav of ordinary soil interspersed among them. If the strip is distributed evenly across the sixteen seah, each seah contains one quarter kav of rocks and one sixteenth kav of ordinary soil interspersed among them. Thus four kav of rocks divided into sixteen equal portions gives a quarter kav to each seah, and the fifth kav of level earth divided into sixteen gives one sixteenth kav to each. See the Perishah for a fuller explanation.

Or a minority of them within a majority. Maimoniyot is also printed with "or," but the Maggid Mishneh writes that the correct text is "and a minority of them within a majority." This is also Rashbam's and the Tur's version of the Gemara. The meaning is as follows. The four kav of rocky ground are distributed in a long narrow strip throughout sixteen se'ah of the field, with one kav of ordinary soil separating them, as explained above. If the strip were perfectly even, each beit se'ah would contain one quarter kav of rocks. The question concerns a strip that is not fully even: in one place it is somewhat wider than the proportional measure, and in another somewhat narrower, so that a majority of the rocks, namely nine quarter-kav units out of the sixteen, extend through a minority of the majority portion of the field, meaning seven beit se'ah, while the minority of the rocks, seven quarter-kav units, extend through the majority of the sixteen beit se'ah, namely nine beit se'ah. This is an unresolved question in the Gemara and therefore the burden of proof rests on the claimant. The Gemara does not ask what the law is if half the rocks are in one half of the field and the other half in the other half, because when the visible disparity does not reach a true majority, it is obvious that there is no significant objection. See the Perishah.
Like a straight line. In that configuration the plow cannot enter between the rocks to plow from one side to the other. Rashbam. From this we learn that what was stated above, that the rocks are "swallowed within the majority of the field," meaning spread in a strip across sixteen beit se'ah with one kav of level ground between them, does not mean that the kav of level ground is divided into, for example, one hundred tiny pieces so that the plow cannot pass through each open portion. If so, this would be the very question the Gemara raises here. Rather, the kav of level ground is scattered among the rocks in the strip in such a way that the plow can enter between each section. This is clear. See the Tur, whose printed versions read: "Likewise the question was raised if they stand in a circle or in many rows alongside one another." It appears that "in many rows" is a scribal error and should read "in a row," meaning a single line with many rocks beside one another so that the plow cannot pass between them. See the Perishah.
Or like a circle or a triangle. In all these configurations the plow cannot easily enter among them. Rashbam. Know that the Gemara arranges the questions in this order: like a ring, meaning a circle, what is the law; like a row, what is the law, etc. Rashbam explains that these questions are presented as sequential "if you say" inquiries: if a circle can be cultivated, what is the law with a row, and so forth, with each later form less cultivable than the previous one. The wording of Rambam and the Mechaber, however, places a row before a circle, and therefore cannot be explained in that sequence.
Or they were at the sides. Maggid Mishneh explains: imagine the rocks clustered in the center, with projections extending from the rocky mass in various directions and the field entering between those projections. The question is whether they are considered dispersed because the field penetrates between the projections, or clustered because the projections remain attached to the main rocky body without any full separation.
Or they followed a winding path. Maggid Mishneh explains that the rocks are attached to one another along a winding line, with parts of the field entering into the bends. Rashbam had different versions and a different explanation. See there.
And the burden of proof rests on the claimant. The Tur writes: therefore, if the purchaser already paid the money, he must accept them; if he has not yet paid, he need not accept them.

Note: See Beit Yosef, who writes in the name of the Ran, Rashba, and Nimukei Yosef that this applies specifically where he says "fields," "my field," or "the fields of so and so." But if he says "all my fields," all are included. If he says "the fields of so and so," it may likewise be that all are included, though some disagree. If he says "the fields that are mine" or "that belong to so and so," using the definite article, all are included. In Shitah Mekubetzet to Bava Batra, Rabbeinu Yonah is cited as reconciling in this manner the sugya of one who sells a house with the sugya in the chapter Mi Shemet. Here the case is where he says "all the property of the house of Rabbi Chiya," and therefore the word "all" is required. In Mi Shemet, however, the case is where he says "my property to so and so," in which formulation all is included. See there.

baer_hetev.he:
יותר. כן הגיה הסמ"ע מכח קושייתו מהרשב"ם ע"ש והש"ך כת' דנ"ל דהרמ"א איירי כאן בכל ענין אפי' אינו מובלע בתוך ה' קבין ובתוך רובה של שדה אבל ד' קבין צריך שיהא דוקא בכל התנאים הנ"ל כי להרשב"ם דינא דבית כור לא עדיף אלא לענין שנמדדין אפי' גבוהין אבל בכל דבר הוא דומה לנדון דלעיל ועיין בטור ויבורר נ"ל ודוק עכ"ל:
עומד. דכל שהוא עומד בתוכו וידוע שבית כור עפר זה מוכר לו אע"פ שלא דקדק לו' בשעת הקנייה בית כור זה ה"ל כאומר הן חסר הן יתר וכן הוכיחו התוס' והרא"ש מהש"ס. סמ"ע:
ומחצה. כשיעור זה מגיע כשמוכר כור ביחד שהוא שלשים בית סאה ואז מגיע רובע הקב לבית סאה וה"ה לפי ערך זה כפי ריבוי או מיעוט הבית סאין שמוכר לו וכמו שיתבאר שם:
baer_hetev.en:

And I'm going to call him." Dr. Yitzhak Shakikaki, who is less than here, is called ‘And Kai Dr. Isaac ate the gift. “But the words of the Rambam and our books are:

meirat_einayim.he:
וי"א דוקא שאין בהן ד' קבין כתב זה בל' י"א אע"ג דהמחבר לפני זה לא הזכיר שבאומר כבית כור דאפי' ד' קבין ויותר נמדדין עמו (וכל' המחבר הוא ג"כ ל' הרמב"ם שם פכ"ח) משום דהטור כתב דמלשון הרמב"ם יראה דאם אמר כבית כור אז בכל ענין נמדד עמו וס"ל דמדקבע הרמב"ם דין זה אחר כל דינים הנ"ל כאלו אמר כל הני דינים המה דוקא בא"ל בית כור אני מוכר לך אבל אם אמר כבית כור בכל ענין נמדדין עמה קמ"ל דיש חולקין ע"ז וס"ל דדוקא לענין גובה או עומק הוא דיש חילוק בין אומר בית כור לאומר כבית כור אבל לענין אם הם יתר מד' קבין אין חילוק והי"א הלזה דכתב הוא מ"ש הטור בס"ד בשם הרשב"ם ומסיק דהרמב"ם פליג עליה (וכנ"ל) ושהרא"ש הסכים לסברא הראשונה אלא שקשה ששם בטור בס"ד כ' בשם רשב"ם דגם באומר כבית כור צריך שלא יהא בו יותר מד' קבין אבל ד' קבין אפי' באומר בית כור עפר אני מוכר לך ואינו גבוה עשרה כו' נמדד עמה וא"כ קשה על מורי ורבי רבי משה איסרלש ז"ל שכ' די"א דוקא שאין בהן ד' קבין. לכן נראה להגיה בדברי מורי ורבי ר' משה דצריך להיות ויש אומרים דוקא שאין בהן יותר מד' קבין ור"ל ולאפוקי מדעת הרמב"ם וכנ"ל ודוק:
אבל אם עומד בתוך השדה כו'. דכל שהוא עומד בתוכו ויודע שבית כור עפר זה מוכר לו אעפ"י שלא דקדק לומר בשעת הקנייה בית כור זה הוה ליה כאומר הן חסר הן יתיר וזה הוכיחו התוספות והרא"ש מהגמרא וע' דרישה:
שבעה קבין ומחצה כשיעור זה מגיע כשמוכר כור ביחד שהוא שלשים בית סאה ואזי מגיע רובע הקב לבית סאה והוא הדין לפי ערך זה לפי ריבוי או מיעוט הבית סאין שמוכר לו וכמו שיתבאר:
meirat_einayim.en:
Some say specifically when they do not contain four kav. Rama writes this as an alternative view even though the Mechaber did not explicitly say that when one says “approximately a beit kor,” even four kav or more are measured with it. The Mechaber follows the Rambam in chapter 28. The Tur understands from the Rambam's placement of this rule after all the earlier laws that the preceding limitations apply only when the seller says “I sell you a beit kor,” whereas if he says “approximately a beit kor,” all irregularities are measured with it. Rama therefore teaches that some disagree and hold that the distinction between “a beit kor” and “approximately a beit kor” concerns only height and depth, not an excess beyond four kav. This alternative view is what the Tur cites in Rashbam's name. The Rosh agrees with that first position. Yet the Tur there says that even when one says “approximately a beit kor,” it must not contain more than four kav, while exactly four kav can be measured even where he says simply “a beit kor of earth.” It is therefore difficult that Rama writes “specifically when they do not contain four kav.” It appears that the text should read, “specifically when they do not contain more than four kav,” thereby excluding the Rambam's broader view.
But if you stand in the field. It is all that he stands in and knows that this dusty reactor is known to him as a non-quirk to say at the time of purchasing this reactor was given to me as saying they were lacking, and this proved the additions and the Rashi of the final and the demand:

siftei_kohen.he: וי"א דוקא שאין בהם ד' קבין. הקשה בסמ"ע הא כ' רשב"ם בעל סברא זו דוקא ביותר מד' קבין אבל ד' קבין נמדדים ולכך הגיה כך ול"נ דמהרמ"א איירי כאן בכל ענין אפילו אינו מובלע בתוך ה' קבין ובתוך רובה של שדה אבל ד' קבין צריך שיהא דוקא בכל התנאים הנזכרים לעיל כי להרשב"ם דינא דבית [דכבית] כור לא עדיף אלא לענין שנמדדים אפילו גבוהין אבל בכל דבר הוא דומה לנדון דלעיל וע' בטור ויבורר נ"ל ודוק:
siftei_kohen.en: And some say, specifically when they do not contain four kav. The Sema asks that Rashbam, whose view this is, writes specifically more than four kav, whereas four kav are measured together with the field, and he therefore emends the text. It appears to me that the Rama here speaks in every circumstance, even where the area is not absorbed within five kav or within most of the field. Four kav, however, are included only when all the conditions stated above are present. According to Rashbam, the rule of a beit kor is superior only in that elevated areas are still measured with it, but in every other respect it follows the preceding rule. See the Tur, where this becomes clear.

mechaber.he: האומר לחבירו בית כור עפר אני מוכר לך מדה בחבל אם פיחת כל שהוא מנכה לו מן הדמים ואם הותיר כל שהוא יחזיר לו:

baer_hetev.he: מנכה. ול"ד למ"ש הט"ו בר"ס רל"ב דכל דבר שנמכר במדה אפילו לית ביה שיעור אונאה המקח בטל דהתם דוקא כשהטעהו וא"ל שהוא כך וכך מדות ולא נמצא כן אבל הכא לא א"ל בבירור שהוא כך וכך אלא א"ל שימדדו אם הוא בית כור כמו שהוא סבור ואם ימצא פחות מזה ינכה לו מהדמים כ"כ התו'. שם:
baer_hetev.en: He deducts. This is unlike the ruling at the beginning of siman 232 that whenever something is sold by measure, a discrepancy voids the sale even if it is less than the ordinary measure of onaah. There, the seller explicitly misrepresented the quantity as a specific measure and it turned out otherwise. Here, however, he did not state with certainty that it contained that quantity. Rather, he said that it should be measured to determine whether it was a beit-kor as he believed, and if less were found the price would be reduced accordingly. So write Tosafot. Ibid.

Less than nine kav. Nine kav is the minimum measure of a field, as the Tur writes in this seif. It appears that although this seif too is taken from Rambam, the present clause concerns a rule with which Rashbam and the Tur also agree. The phrase "less than nine kav" here includes the quarter-kav allowances. For example, if he sold forty-four se'ah, the permitted excess would be thirty-five quarter-kav units. Proportionately this is more than one quarter kav per beit se'ah, yet it still does not reach the minimum independent field size until the excess reaches thirty-six quarter-kav units, which equals nine kav. The Tur writes this; see there. The phrase "to strengthen the seller's position" refers to the rule that the purchaser must pay money for the excess, not to a change in market price. In the following seif Rambam's distinctive view begins: even if the excess together with the permitted quarter-kav allowances reaches nine kav, the purchaser must still repay in money if the market price changed, as explained there.
To strengthen the seller's position. Meaning, the rule requiring money is for the seller's benefit. If the seller instead wishes to take back the excess land itself, the purchaser must return it. The Tur writes in the name of Rashbam that the distinction between less than nine kav and nine kav applies only to an excess beyond the agreed measure. If the seller delivered less than the agreed amount by more than one quarter kav per beit se'ah, he always deducts from the purchase price. Since this field contains no additional land, we cannot obligate the seller to give the purchaser land from elsewhere. It appears that the same applies if the seller wishes to supply the deficiency from another field: the purchaser can say, "What use do I have for a separate tiny field like this?" The seller must therefore deduct from the price. These are the Tur's words.

היתה התוספות יתירה כו'. שמפ' מ"ש ואי איכא מילתא יתירא ט' קבין הדר כמ"ש הרשב"ם שם וי"מ ואי איכא יתירות כו' שצריך כו' ע"ש ומש"ש התם כגון דהוה יקירא כו' מפרש אם היתה התוספת ט' קבין על היתירות דמחזיר הלוקח קרקע אמרינן ליה ר"ל ללוקח והכל ליפות כחו של מוכר ולטובתו דהא בשעת המכירה היתה ביוקר וברשות הלוקח הוזלה אי מעות נותן למוכר נותן כשעת היוקר בתחלה ואי קרקע נותן לו כזולא דהשתא דאין המוכר מחוייב ליקח כמו שהיה בתחלה ואם רוצה ליתן לו מעות אז כופין את המוכר למכור דאין הלוקח מחוייב ליתו לו קרקע בע"כ כזולא דהשתא ופריך והתניא כשהוא נותן כו' ר"ל הלוקח למוכר ומשני התם כגון כו' והכל לטובת המוכר ובכה"ג לייפות כחו של מוכר וברצונו הדבר תלוי שאם רוצה מחזיר לו קרקע הואיל ואין הפסד ללוקח שמחזיר לו כמו שמכרה לו ולפי' מיושב מ"ש אי ארעא יהבת ליה ומיושב ג"כ כופין את המוכר למכור ואת כו' ומיושב מתני' ג"כ דלעולם לייפות כחו של מוכר אמרינן:
ונותנו לו כו'. בד"א כו'. הכל לשון הגמ':
beur_hagra.en:
If the excess was greater, etc. He explains the Gemara's statement that if there is an additional significant amount of nine kav the land is returned, following Rashbam. Others explain that if the excess itself reaches the stated measure, the purchaser must return land. The subsequent discussion, 'there, where it had been expensive, etc.,' means that if the excess is nine kav and the purchaser must return land, the court addresses the purchaser. Everything is arranged to strengthen the seller's position. Since the land was expensive at the time of sale and became cheaper while in the purchaser's possession, if the purchaser returns money he pays according to the original high price; if he returns land, he returns according to its present lower value, because the seller is not compelled to accept the land on the former terms. If the purchaser wishes to pay money, the seller is compelled to sell the excess, because the purchaser cannot be forced to return land at its present low value. The baraita's wording is then explained consistently, all for the seller's benefit. This also resolves the phrases 'if you give him land,' 'we compel the seller to sell,' and the Mishna's general formulation.

היתה התוספות יתירה על ט' קבין כו'. המחבר כ' להלכה דברי הרמב"ם מכאן עד סעיף י"ג ודלא כמ"ש הטור עם פירש"י והרמב"ם כ"כ ע"פ פירושו לסוגיות הגמ' וכבר הארכתי בזה בדרישה ונתתי טעם לדבריו שמשמעות סוגיא דגמרא הוא כדבריו. ושלפירוש ר"ש והטור צריכין לדחוק באותן המקומות בגמרא וסלקתי ממנו תמיהת המגיד משנה ושל מור"ם שהניחו להרמב"ם בצ"ע ע"ש. וכאן אקצר ואכתוב כלל כוונת הרמב"ם והוא זה דס"ל להלכה בזה גם כן כהטור דרובע לבית סאה ניתן למחילה באומר הן חסר והן יתיר וטפי לא ושאם הוא יתר מרובע לבית סאה צריכין להחזיר גם הרבעין עצמן ושיד המוכר בו על העליונה בכל זה ס"ל להרמב"ם כהטור וכר"ש אלא שמחולק עמהן באם הוא יותר מרובע קב לבית סאה והגיע היתרון עם הרבעין לט' קבין דלר"ש והטור אין בזה יד המוכר על העליונה אלא אם ירצה הלוקח מחזיר לו הקרקע בעינו בע"כ דמוכר והרמב"ם ס"ל דגם בכה"ג יד המוכר על העליונה אא"כ היה יתרון כ"כ שאחר שנתת לכל בית סאה רובע ישאר בהיתר עוד ט' קבין ובזה דוקא אמרו שמחזיר לו הקרקע בעינו בע"כ ומטעם שאכתוב בסמוך ואפי' כשהיתרון כ"כ הרבה ס"ל דעדיין יד הלוקח אינה על העליונה עכ"פ ואם היתה הקרקע מתחלה בשעת הקניה ביוקר ועכשיו בשעת החזרה עומדת בזול אין ביד הלוקח רשות להחזיר לו היתרון בקרקע בעינו אלא צריך ליתן בעדה כ"כ דמים כמו שהיתה שוה בשעת הקנין או מחזיר לו קרקע בשער הזול כשיעור אותן דמים שהיו שוו היתרונות בשעת הקנין דא"ל המוכר ברשותך ובמזלך עמדו בזול הקרקעות ואם היה בהיפוך שהיו בזול בשעת הקנין ועכשיו בשעת חזרה נתייקרו אמרינן אדרבה דברשות מוכר נתייקרו דהיתרונו' לא נמכרו לו מעול' נמצא כלל דבריו דלעולם יד המוכר על העליונה זולת אם הקרקעות במקח הראשון דאז צריך לקבל הקרקע ודוקא כשהיו בהיתרונות כ"כ שהיה יתרון ט' קבין נוסף על הרבעין של כל סאה וסאה וכל זה כתב ע"פ משמעות הסוגיא כמ"ש בדרישה ובאמת לא מצאתי טעם נכון לדבריו גם המ"מ ומור"ם ז"ל תמהו בזה עליו דכיון דעכ"פ נשאר ט' קבין והוא ראוי לשיעור שדה וראוי להמוכר למה יהיה ידו על העליונה לכוף להלוקח ליתן לו דמים בעדו ויש לדחוק וליישב זה ולומר דה"ט כיון דהרביעית לבית סאה נתנו למחילה מ"ה אף כשיש יתרון עליהם עד שבין כולם הוא ט' קבין מ"מ אינו כדאי להיות להן דין חזרת קרקע בע"כ של המוכר דיאמר לו המוכר אלו לא היה היתרון היה תופס בהן הלוקח בהרביעית בחנם באמרו שהן בכלל מקח שקנה עכשיו שיש יתרון יתנם לי בע"כ גם אני אומר שהן בכלל הקנין לענין זה שאינו יכול להכריחני ליקחם מידי בעינו אלא ישלם לי דמיהן כמו ששילם לי גוף השדה עד שיהי' נוסף על כל הרבעין ט' קבין דאז ה"ל כאלו יש לו שדה סמוכה אצלו וק"ל. אלו הן כלל דברי הרמב"ם ועפ"ז יתבארו לך פרטי דברי המחבר שהן הן הדברי' אות באות כמ"ש הרמב"ם:
נותנין רובע לכל סאה כו'. אין ר"ל דהרבעים ישארו ללוקח אלא כלו' נותנין ומחשבין ורואין אם לאחר שיחלוק מהיתרון רובע לכל בית סאה ישאר עוד ט' קבין אז יש כח ביד הלוקח להחזיר להמוכר הכל יחד בקרקע בעינו ואין צריך ליתן לו בעדו דמים:
meirat_einayim.en:
If the excess was more than nine kav, etc. From here through seif 13 the Mechaber rules according to the Rambam, unlike the Tur's explanation following Rashi. I discussed this at length in the Derishah and showed that the flow of the Gemara supports the Rambam, while Rashbam and the Tur must force several passages. I also answered the Maggid Mishneh and Rama's objections. Here I will state only the Rambam's general method. He agrees with the Tur that where the seller says “more or less,” a quarter kav per seah is waived, but no more. If the excess exceeds that amount, even the quarter kav amounts themselves must be returned. He also agrees that in this general area the seller has the stronger hand. The dispute concerns a case where the excess beyond a quarter kav per seah, together with the waived quarters themselves, reaches nine kav. Rashbam and the Tur hold that once the total reaches nine kav, the seller no longer has the stronger hand. The purchaser may return the actual land even against the seller's will. The Rambam holds that the seller still has the stronger hand unless, after allocating a quarter kav to each seah as the ordinary waived amount, there remain a full additional nine kav beyond all those quarters. Only then must the seller take back the land itself even against his will. Even where the excess is that large, however, the purchaser still does not always have the stronger hand as to valuation. If land was expensive at the time of sale and is cheap when the excess is returned, the purchaser cannot simply return the excess land at its present low value. He must pay its value as of the original sale, or return at the present cheap rate enough land to equal that original value. The seller can say that the fall in land values occurred in the purchaser's domain and fortune. Conversely, if land was cheap at the sale and has become expensive, the seller benefits from the increase, because the excess was never sold to the purchaser. Thus, according to the Rambam, the seller's hand is generally stronger. Only when values remain as at the original transaction, and only where the additional excess beyond all the quarter kav portions is itself nine kav, is the seller compelled to take back the actual land. I have not found a fully satisfying rationale for the Rambam, and the Maggid Mishneh and Rama also question why, if nine kav remain and constitute a field in their own right, the seller should be able to force the purchaser to pay money instead of returning the land. One can answer with difficulty as follows. Since a quarter kav per seah is ordinarily waived, even when some excess is added and the combined total reaches nine kav, the seller can say: Had there been no added excess, you would have kept those quarter kav portions without payment as part of your purchase. Now that there is excess, you cannot reverse matters and force me to take back those same waived portions as land. I may instead treat them as part of the transaction and demand their value like the rest of the field. Only when there are nine kav beyond all the ordinarily waived quarters is there a distinct field-like excess that must be returned in kind. This is the general approach of the Rambam, and on this basis the details of the Mechaber's language, which closely follows him, can be understood.

meirat_einayim.he:
ומ"ש בד"א כו' ר"ל בד"א דיד הלוקח על העליונה ונותנה לו כשעה שלקחו ממנו:
כשהיתה בזול כו'. ה"ה דהוי מצי למימר כשעמד הקרקע בשער הראשון אלא דהרמב"ם תפס לשון הברייתא והגמרא דאיירי שם כשלא עמדו בשער א' ומה"נ סיים בסעיף שלפני זה וכתב דנותנו לו כשעה שלקחה ממנו משום דאיירי גם שם בגמרא כשנשתנה השער. ומ"ש שאם הותיר כו' "עד אינו מחזיר לו אלא דמים ר"ל דיד מוכר על העליונה וכמ"ש בס"ט בשדה דפחות מט' קבין מחזיר לו דמים ליפות כח המוכר וכמ"ש שם. ומ"ש הותיר חצי קב כו' עד בדמי' ר"ל אם עמדה בזול צריך ליתן לו דמי שוויה כמו שהיה בשעת הקנין או קרקע בזול כשעת החזרה וכנ"ל בדין שדה ומ"ש מור"ם בהג"ה ז"ל כל מ"ש מתחלת ס"ט כו' היינו משום דסבירא ליה למור"ם דמ"ש בס"ט אם היה התוספות פחות מט' קבין כו' ר"ל אפי' היה בו ט' קבין אלא שבלא הרבעים אינו ט' קבין אפ"ה צריך להחזיר לו דמים וכנ"ל ומ"ה כתב דז"א אלא לדברי הרמב"ם אבל לעד"נ כמ"ש לעיל דמ"ש בס"ח קאי אפי' לפי' ר"ש והטור ומתחלה כתב דבר הפשוט דבזה דאין בו שיעור שדה צריך ליתן דמים ליפות כח המוכר ושאפ"ה אם יש להמוכר שדה בצדו מחזיק לו קרקע ואח"כ כתב לרבותא דאפי' יש בו ט' קבין עם הרבעין (אם אין לו שדה בצדו) צריך ליתן לו דמים וק"ל ומ"ש מור"ם דמסעיף ט' עד כאן הוא לשון הרמב"ם צ"ע למה כתב עד כאן שהוא סי"ב הא גם סי"ב אזיל דוקא לשיטת הרמב"ם ולא לפי' ר"ש והטור וכמ"ש פירושו לפני זה וצ"ל שהוא ט"ס שנפל בדפוס והג"ה זו צריכה להיות מסודרת אחר סעיף י"ב ושם שפיר שייך לומר עד כאן ור"ל עד סעיף י"ג ודו"ק:
meirat_einayim.en:
What he writes, "When does this apply," etc. Meaning, when does the preceding rule apply that the purchaser has the stronger position and gives the seller according to the value at the time he bought it?
When the land had been inexpensive, etc. The same law could have been stated where the market price remained unchanged. Rambam merely uses the wording of the baraita and Gemara, which discuss a change in price. For the same reason the preceding seif concludes that the purchaser gives according to the value at the time he bought it, because the Gemara there likewise discusses a changed market price. What Rambam writes, "if there was an excess, etc., he returns only money," means that the seller has the stronger position, as explained in seif 9 concerning a field where the excess is less than nine kav: he returns money in order to strengthen the seller's position. What he writes, "if the excess was half a kav, etc., in money," means that if the land became cheaper, he must give money according to its value at the time of acquisition, or return cheap land according to the value at the time of return, as explained above concerning a field. Rama's gloss, "everything written from the beginning of seif 9, etc.," is based on his understanding that seif 9's phrase "if the excess was less than nine kav" includes even a case where there are nine kav with the quarter-kav allowances but not nine kav apart from those allowances. Therefore Rama says that this is only Rambam's view. In my humble opinion, however, the correct explanation is as I wrote above: seif 8 states a rule accepted even by Rashbam and the Tur, first giving the straightforward case where the excess is not a field-sized amount, so money must be paid to strengthen the seller; even so, if the seller owns an adjoining field he can take land. Rambam then adds a greater novelty: even where the excess reaches nine kav together with the quarter-kav allowances, if the seller has no adjoining field the purchaser must pay money. This is clear. Rama further writes that from seif 9 until "here" is Rambam's wording. This requires study. Why does he write "until here," meaning through seif 12, when seif 12 too follows specifically Rambam's approach and not that of Rashbam and the Tur, as I explained above? One must say that a typographical error occurred and the gloss should be placed after seif 12. There the phrase "until here" is appropriate, meaning until seif 13. Examine carefully.

mechaber.he: דין חצי קב בגינה כדין ט' קבין בשדה שאם הותיר בגינה פחות מחצי קב על הרבעים אינו מחזיר לו אלא דמים הותיר חצי קב מחזיר לו כל הרבעים עם היתר בדמים או קרקע כשעת הזול של עת החזרה (וכל מ"ש מתחלת סעיף ט' ע"כ הוא ל' הרמב"ם פכ"ח מה' מכירה והמ"מ הניחו שם בצ"ע והעיקר כדעת י"א כי כל שהוא פחות מט' קבין הרשות ביד המוכר ליקח קרקע או מעות ואם נותן לו מעות נותן כשעת הזול בין היתה בזול והוקרה או היתה ביוקר והוזלה אבל היתה לו שדה אחרת סמוכה לתוספת זה נותן לו קרקע וכן אם היתה התוספת ט' קבין ומחשבין כל המותר בין הרבעים בין הנשאר) (טור):
mechaber.en: In a garden, one-half kav has the same status as nine kav in a field. Thus, if the excess beyond the permitted quarter-kav units is less than one-half kav, the purchaser returns only money. If the excess reaches one-half kav, he returns all the quarter-kav units together with the excess, either in money or land, valued at the lower price prevailing at the time of return. Rama: The principal ruling is that whenever the excess is less than nine kav, the seller may choose land or money. If he takes money, it is valued at the lower price, whether the land was cheap and rose in value or expensive and fell. If the seller owns an adjoining field, the purchaser returns land. Likewise, when the excess is nine kav, all excess is calculated, including both the quarter-kav units and the remainder.

siftei_kohen.en: Or if he said, etc. See the Sema, seifim ketanim 41, 42, and 43. His explanation does not appear correct. The Maggid Mishneh, Beit Yosef, and Ir Shushan correctly explain that the Rambam and Mechaber also agree with Rashbam, and the Sema's objections are unjustified. The Bach likewise explains that the Rambam means that the purchaser receives according to the less favorable wording, whether the land is deficient or excessive, and he rejects the Tur and Sema. I also found an express contradiction to the Sema in the Rambam's commentary to the Mishna in the chapter Beit Kor: the purchaser receives the smaller of the stated measurements, and this is the meaning of following the less favorable expression. Thus the less favorable wording always disadvantages the purchaser and means the lesser measurement, not, as the Sema explains, the wording that diminishes the seller's first statement. The Sema's explanation is also difficult because the source Mishna never mentions the phrase 'a beit kor.' Clearly the Rambam and Mechaber use that phrase here only as an illustration of the expression 'measured by a rope,' and their intent accords with the Raavad, whose words follow. It appears that Ri Migash, Rashi, and Rashbam likewise agree with the Raavad, whose ruling is correct: the less favorable wording is applied as a leniency for the defendant. If the buyer has already paid, he is the claimant. If he has not paid, possesses the land, and the seller claims additional money, the seller is the claimant. Depending upon the case, a deficiency or an excess may be either favorable or unfavorable to the defendant. The Maggid Mishneh writes that even where the seller comes to collect money, the purchaser is compelled to pay for an excess because land remains in its owner's presumptive possession, just as is said regarding contradictory language in a rental, as explained in chapter 7 of Hilchot Sechirut. He plainly does not mean that the purchaser is forced to pay if he does not want the excess land, for presumptive ownership has no relevance there. Likewise, in the rental case one pays for the thirteenth month only after having occupied it, as explained below in siman 312:15. Rather, he means that if the purchaser wishes to retain the entire parcel but refuses to pay for the excess, he is compelled to pay, and until payment the entire land remains the seller's because land stands in its owner's presumptive possession. The Maggid Mishneh says this because the Raavad's plain language, 'the seller claims the additional money,' might suggest otherwise. In my opinion, the Raavad agrees and speaks only where the purchaser wishes the land to remain his and the seller merely claims payment for the excess; in that situation the law may favor the purchaser according to the less favorable wording. It is also possible that the Maggid Mishneh understood the Raavad this way and came only to clarify his intent. Examine carefully.

פיחת יתר על שתות ינכה פי' ינכה כל הפחת אף השתות כדין פיחת יתר מרובע הנ"ל בהן חסר או יתיר וכ"כ הטור אחר זה בהיותו יותר משתות דיתן לו דמים אף בעד השתות וכתבו הטור שם משום דכתב עליו דינא באם היתה היתרון פחות מט' קבין שיתן לו דמים או קרקע כו' ובחסרון אינו נותן לו המוכר קרקע ממקום אחר רק דמים צריך ליתן בעד הפחת כמ"ש לעיל:
meirat_einayim.en:
He said to him, "with its identifying marks and boundaries," etc. The Tur's wording is: "I am selling you a beit kor of land as it stands within its marks and boundaries," etc. In the Perishah I wrote that the Tur carefully adds "as it stands" because the case requires that the seller stand within the field, or say "this beit kor," and also say, "Take it within its boundaries and signs." Only then is there extra language. If he stands within it or says "this," the law would otherwise be that an ordinary deficiency or excess is accepted, as explained in seif 8. By adding, "take it within its marks and boundaries," he adds a special qualification, and therefore we say that a disparity up to one sixth is accepted. The Tur alludes to this by writing "as it stands," meaning he says "this" or physically stands within it. See the Perishah. This is unlike the Levush, who copies Rashbam's wording in a way that leaves room for error.
If the deficiency exceeds one sixth, he deducts. Meaning, he deducts the entire deficiency, including the first one sixth, just as where a deficiency exceeds one quarter kav per beit se'ah under the language "more or less," the entire amount is deducted. The Tur likewise writes below that where the excess is greater than one sixth, the purchaser pays money even for the first one sixth. The Tur mentions that there because he proceeds to discuss a case where the excess is less than nine kav and the purchaser must give money or land. With a deficiency, however, the seller does not supply land from elsewhere; he deducts money for the entire deficiency, as explained above.

ketzot_hachoshen.en:
A particular beit kor. In the next seif the Shulchan Aruch speaks of "a particular place" or "this orchard." The implication is that if one sold merely "an orchard" or "a beit kor" without identifying a particular one, the seller cannot later say, "I sold you only the name," and must provide a complete orchard or a full beit kor. Beit Yosef explains that Rambam and Tur intentionally wrote "a particular beit kor" or "an orchard I have in such and such a place," because without such identification there is no basis to say that only the name was sold.
Bach was troubled by this, arguing that even without saying "this" or identifying the location, perhaps the seller should still be able to say, "I sold you only the name." In my view Rambam holds that the doctrine of selling merely the name applies specifically where the seller said "this," or identified a particular place in a manner equivalent to "this." Ritva in Perek HaMekabel writes that the case is one where the seller said, "this beit kor of earth." Since he identified this parcel, if the parcel is commonly called by that name, the purchaser must accept it even if it does not contain the full measure. Ritva notes that this is the reading of Raavad. Rambam follows the same text. If the purchaser says to the seller, "Sell me a beit kor," whether the seller can still answer, "I sold you merely something bearing that name," depends on the dispute in siman 321. Rif, Rambam, and Rosh do not distinguish whether the lessor said the formula to the lessee or the lessee to the lessor, and under their view the same doctrine can apply here. Rabbi Meir HaLevi Abulafia, Ramban, and Rashba distinguish where the lessee initiated the formulation, and according to them a purchaser who requested a full beit kor would not be subject to the mere name defense. See what I wrote there.

My property. Even if he said 'all.' So writes the Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah. It appears that his reason is that Rabbeinu Yonah concludes: 'But one who says, All my property I sell, includes movable property as well.' Why did he need the word 'all'? It must be intended as a distinction, namely that regarding 'the property of the house of Chiya,' even saying 'all' does not help. In my humble opinion this is strained. It appears more likely that the word 'all' is a scribal error. Alternatively, one may explain that he means: 'But one who says, All the property of the house of Chiya I sell to you, includes movable property as well.' If so, Rabbeinu Yonah may be reconciling Rashbam's words. Ibid.

And specifically where he said “fields,” etc. This gloss belongs here. A printing error placed it in seif 10. It comments on the Mechaber's rule that if one says, “All my fields,” even three or four are included, but gardens and orchards are excluded. Rama then adds that this is specifically when he said “fields.” This follows Rabbeinu Yonah, cited by the Tur, who writes that if he uses the expression “all my landholdings,” everything is included, even orchards and houses. From there we learn that when Rama says, “but if he said land,” he means “all my land,” in the wording of Rabbeinu Yonah. Still, it is possible that even if he says merely “lands,” without “all,” and he owns only one field and one orchard, the orchard is included, because he used the plural “lands” and these are his only two parcels, while an orchard is legally land. Perhaps for this reason Rama omitted the word “all.”

pitchei_teshuva.en: All lands. See Responsa Rabbi Akiva Eiger, end of siman 129. The word "all" is not inherently necessary to include houses within the term "land." It is needed here only because without it the grant would otherwise be limited to two parcels. In ordinary usage, houses are included in land even without the word "all." Although the Tur in siman 95 cites the Itur that something detached and later attached remains classified as movable, either houses are different, as the Shach writes there, or in common speech houses are included in the term land. See there.

[" אפילו בתים. כ\"כ ג\"כ הטור ויש לספק אם העבדים בכלל סתם קרקעות עכ\"ל סמ\"ע ולא ידענא מאי מספקא ליה הא פשיטא דאינם בכלל מקרקעי אלא בכלל מטלטלי וכדלקמן סי' רמ\"ח ס\"י:"]
[" וכל המטלטלים כו'. אע\"ג דלקמן סי' רמ\"ח סעיף י\"א כל המטלטלים בכלל נכסי אע\"פ שלא אמר כל שאני התם דמתנה בעין יפה נותן וחילוק זה מוזכר בתוס' והרא\"ש והר\"ן וכן נ\"ל לדעת הרמב\"ם והמחבר (וכ\"כ הב\"ח אבל שאר תירוצי' שהוזכרו בתו' ושאר פוסקים קשה להו לומ' בדעת הרמב\"ם והמחבר) ומ\"ש הרב המגיד על דברי הרמב\"ם דכאן באומר כל נכסי המטלטלים בכלל כמ\"ש המחבר והכי מוכח בפרק מ\"ש ואמרינן התם דאפילו תפילין איקרי נכסי כו' אע\"ג דבפרק מ\"ש במתנה איירי ה\"ק דבפ' מ\"ש מוכח דכל המטלטלי' איקרי ניכסי ואפילו תפילין וכה\"ג וא\"כ נהי דהתם במתנה מ\"מ כיון דהכל בכלל נכסי כאן שאמר כל נכסי כל המטלטלים בכלל דנהי דמוכר בעין רעה מוכר היינו היכא שלא אמר כל ואי לאו הך דפרק מ\"ש אפי' אמר כל לא הוי כל המטלטלים בכלל דמאן לימא לן דאיקרי נכסי כלל כן נ\"ל ודוק:"]
[" אבל אמר נכסי דבי פלניא כו'. אפילו אמר כל כן כתב הטור בשם הר\"ר יונה ונראה שטעמו מדכתב ה\"ר יונה בסוף דבריו אבל האומר כל נכסי אני מוכר גם המטלטלים בכלל דלאיזה צורך הזכיר כל אלא לדיוקא אצטריך דבנכסי דבי חייא אפילו כל לא מהני אבל לפע\"ד זה דוחק ויותר נראה דתיבת כל ט\"ס הוא או י\"ל דה\"ק אבל האו' כל נכסי דבי חייא אני מוכר לך גם המטלטלים בכלל וא\"כ י\"ל דה\"ר יונה מתרץ דברי רשב\"ם ודוק:"]
siftei_kohen.en:

And all movable property, etc. Although below, siman 248, seif 11, all movable property is included in the term 'my assets' even when he did not say 'all,' that case concerns a gift, and one who gives a gift gives generously. This distinction is mentioned by Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Ran, and in my opinion it is also the view of the Rambam and the Mechaber. The Bach likewise writes this, while the other answers mentioned by Tosafot and the other poskim are difficult to attribute to the Rambam and the Mechaber. The Maggid Mishneh writes concerning the Rambam that here, where one says 'all my assets,' movable property is included, as the Mechaber writes, and that this is proved in the chapter Mi SheMet, where the Gemara states that even tefillin are called assets. Although that chapter concerns a gift, his meaning is that the chapter proves that all movable property, even tefillin and the like, is called 'assets.' Therefore, although that case is a gift, once everything is included within the term 'assets,' here too, when he said 'all my assets,' all movable property is included. Although a seller is presumed to sell sparingly, that is only where he did not say 'all.' Without the proof from the chapter Mi SheMet, even saying 'all' would not necessarily include every movable item, since we would not know that such items are called assets at all. This appears correct to me. Examine carefully.
But if he said, 'The assets of so and so,' etc. This applies even if he said 'all.' So writes the Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah. His reason appears to be that Rabbeinu Yonah concludes, 'But one who says, I am selling all my assets, includes the movable property as well.' Why did he mention the word 'all'? It must be for the inference that regarding 'the assets of the house of Chiya,' even saying 'all' is ineffective. In my opinion, however, this is strained. It is more likely that the word 'all' is a scribal error. Alternatively, Rabbeinu Yonah may mean: if he said, 'I am selling you all the assets of the house of Chiya,' the movable property is also included. According to this, Rabbeinu Yonah may be reconciling the words of Rashbam. Examine carefully.

mechaber.he: האומר לחבירו שדה ראובן אני מוכר לך וכיון שבא הלוקח להשתמש בה אמר ליה המוכר אינו זו השדה שהיתה של ראובן אלא כך היא קרויה ולעולם לא היתה לו אלא זו שהיתה של ראובן ולקחתיה ממנו והיא שמכרתי לך על המוכר להביא ראיה ואם לא הביא ראיה זוכה הלוקח בזו שכל העם קורין אותה של ראובן:
mechaber.en: If one says, "I am selling you Reuven's field," and when the purchaser seeks to use it the seller says, "This is not the field that formerly belonged to Reuven, but merely a field called by his name. The field that actually belonged to Reuven is this other one, which I bought from him and intended to sell you," the seller bears the burden of proof. If he provides no proof, the purchaser acquires the field universally known as Reuven's field.

beer_hagolah.he:
פ) שם דכ"א עובדא בנכסיה דבר סיסין לקמיה דרב נחמן שם (ריש דף ל') ופסק כרב נחמן וכן בהלכות הרב המגיד:
צ) יביא עדים דלאו מראובן לקחה אלא דאקרויי הוא דמקרי הכי ואוקמי' לה בידי דמוכר דפשיטא לן דהאי דאמר שדה דראובן הכי קאמר שדה שקניתי ממנו ולא שדה שלא קניתי ממנו אעפ"י שנקראין כן מפי' רשב"ם שם:
beer_hagolah.en:
Peh) There, halachah 21, based on the incident concerning the property of Bar Sisin before Rav Nachman, Bava Batra 30a. Rambam rules like Rav Nachman, as does the Rif. See Maggid Mishneh.
Tzadi) The seller must bring witnesses that he did not purchase the field from Reuven and that it merely happens to be called by Reuven's name. Until then the land remains with the seller, because we understand the phrase "Reuven's field" to mean "the field I bought from Reuven," not a field that he never bought from Reuven even if people happen to call it by that name. Rashbam there.

meirat_einayim.he: על המוכר להביא ראיה פי' ראיה דזו לא היתה של ראובן ואם מביא ראיה א"צ לתנו לו אלא האחרת אף שאין קורין אותה ע"ש ראובן דמסתמא האומר שדה ראובן ר"ל השדה שקניתי מראובן וכיון שמביא ראיה שזו לא קנה מראובן לא היה דעתו על זה כן פי' ר"ש פח"ה ריש דף ל"ו ע"ש ולא "כע"ש דכ' שצריך להביא ראיה שמכר לו השדה השניה ע"ש ודו"ק:
meirat_einayim.en: It is not for the seller to bring evidence to him, but to the other hand, that it is not inscribed to him, but that the other person who has not made it clear to him, that the field of the field I have bought from him, and that he has no evidence that it has not been given to him
